title: A Weather for the Undertow
premise: Bram Marchetti, a bridge inspector who measures everything—including the silences in his marriage to the singer Nell—discovers a song on late-night radio that she wrote decades ago and never recorded, a song that names a death their family has spent thirty years pretending was an accident. The song's broadcast means someone else knows: her brother Theo, who took the blame for a fire that killed their father's business partner, is dying and wants the truth on record before he goes. As Bram and Nell drive toward him through a collapsing heat wave, they must decide whether justice outside the law—the confession that could clear Theo but implicate Nell as the one who set the fire—is worth the family they've built on top of the lie. The book ends with Theo's quiet death and a public reckoning Nell chooses freely, leaving Bram to learn that love measured in expansion joints was never holding anything together at all.
about_author: Odile Okonkwo is a former structural engineer who left bridge inspection after eleven years to write fiction about the loads people carry. She lives in a river town where she still can't stop checking the bolts.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. On the Corliss Street Bridge, Bram measures gaps in steel the way he measures gaps in conversation, cataloguing what his marriage has stopped saying. A routine inspection report becomes a private ledger of unsaid things. Emotional beat: tenderness disguised as precision; the reader learns Bram loves by inventory.

chapters.title: The Song That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Driving home from a gig she almost cancelled, Nell hears a voice on the college radio station singing a song she wrote at nineteen and buried—a song about a fire. She pulls over, shaking, and calls no one. Emotional beat: terror arriving as music; the past announcing itself politely.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram finds Nell awake at 3 a.m., listening to a recording of the broadcast on loop. She tells him only that it's 'an old song,' and he pretends to believe her, adding the lie to his mental ledger. Emotional beat: complicity beginning; two people protecting each other into isolation.

chapters.title: Theo's Voice
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. A letter arrives from her brother Theo, postmarked a hospice in Marrow Falls: 'They played it. I asked them to. Come before I can't explain.' Nell burns the letter, then digs it out of the sink. Emotional beat: dread braided with longing; thirty years of exile ending in a summons.

chapters.title: What the Family Arranged Itself Around
chapters.summary: Dual POV, alternating scenes. Flashback woven through present: the 1994 warehouse fire, the partner who died, the father who decided Theo would take the blame as a juvenile, and nineteen-year-old Nell who let him. Emotional beat: the architecture of a lie revealed load-bearing wall by wall.

chapters.title: The Long Detour
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram takes leave without telling his supervisor why, and the couple drives toward Marrow Falls under a heat advisory. In the car, Nell finally says 'It was me' and Bram realizes he'd known, or half-known, for years. Emotional beat: relief and rupture in the same breath.

chapters.title: Radio Silence
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. A radio DJ calls: lawyers for the dead partner's estate have heard the song and are asking questions; the statute may be gone but a civil suit isn't. Nell understands the broadcast wasn't mercy—it was bait. Emotional beat: the trap closing gently, with good intentions on all sides.

chapters.title: Marrow Falls
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. They arrive in the shrunken river town; the hospice, the shuttered foundry, the town that remembers the Marchetti name. Bram inspects the old foundry footbridge out of habit and finds it failing—like everything else here. Emotional beat: homecoming as corrosion.

chapters.title: The Dying Man's Ledger
chapters.summary: Theo's POV (first time). Theo, oxygen tank and old guitar, has spent months writing down the truth he's carried since he was sixteen. He doesn't want forgiveness; he wants the record corrected before the last witness dies. Emotional beat: fierce clarity at the end of a life.

chapters.title: Sister, Arsonist, Widow-to-be
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. First meeting between siblings in thirty years. Theo asks her not to confess—he asked the radio to play the song so she'd come, not so she'd burn. Nell realizes he wants absolution he refuses to accept. Emotional beat: love expressed as mutual protection, which is its own violence.

chapters.title: The Estate's Man
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. A lawyer named Voss finds them at the motel: the partner's daughter wants acknowledgment, not money, and will trade silence for a signed statement. Bram, the man of precise records, sees the offer for what it is—another joint designed to hold weight it can't. Emotional beat: temptation wearing a reasonable face.

chapters.title: Load Test
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Nell plays the song for Theo one full time, both verses, including the verse about who struck the match. Theo weeps and then laughs—the terrible laughter of a debt being named. Emotional beat: catharsis that costs something real.

chapters.title: What Bram Kept
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram confesses his own ledger: he knew about the fire's true cause from a drunk confession on their honeymoon and said nothing for twenty years to keep her. Nell's fury is total. Emotional beat: the marriage's central fracture exposed—not the secret, but the years of managed silence.

chapters.title: The Daughter
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. Nell meets Ruth, the dead partner's daughter, alone, without lawyers. Ruth is not vengeful; she is tired and wants one sentence of truth. Nell gives her more than the sentence and watches it land like weather. Emotional beat: grief recognizing grief across the fault line.

chapters.title: Heat Crack
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The Corliss Street Bridge fails inspection remotely—Bram flags it from a motel room—and a span sags that night; no deaths, but the town where it happened erupts. Bram, the inspector who measures everything, confronts the limits of measurement. Emotional beat: professional identity cracking alongside personal.

chapters.title: Confession, Draft One
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo helps Nell write her statement, editing it like a lyric—cutting self-pity, keeping fact. Their collaboration becomes the truest duet of their lives. Emotional beat: sibling love recovered through craft; justice taking the shape of a well-made thing.

chapters.title: Voss's Last Offer
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Voss raises the stakes: sign the sanitized statement and the family name survives; refuse and Ruth sues the estate Theo barely owns. Bram, for once, chooses imprecision—he tears up the draft. Emotional beat: the careful man's first reckless act, done out of love rather than duty.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. In the hospice garden, Nell records the song properly for the first time, phone propped against a watering can, Theo harmonizing from his wheelchair. She sends it to the radio station with her real name attached. Emotional beat: art as testimony; the unrecorded song finally existing.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, short sections. The broadcast goes out; the town, the father (still alive, furious), the press converge on Marrow Falls. Theo deteriorates rapidly. Nell signs her statement with Ruth beside her. Emotional beat: the climax—truth released and immediately beyond anyone's control, like water.

chapters.title: Last Verse
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo dies at dawn with the song playing softly from a nurse's phone, Nell holding one hand and Bram the other. His final words are an engineering joke about load-bearing. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace; the debt transferred to the living willingly.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Measured
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. No charges—statute expired—but the civil settlement strips the family company, and the father stops speaking to Nell, which she counts as a kind of graduation. Bram returns to bridges, but keeps a new notebook: things actually said. Emotional beat: cost tallied honestly; survival priced and paid.

chapters.title: A Weather for the Undertow
chapters.summary: Nell's POV. A year later, Nell performs the song publicly for the first time, in a small hall, with Ruth in the third row. Bram is in the back with his ledger closed on his knee. The last line lands on the image of swimming past the breakers where the undertow lives. Emotional beat: resolution as ongoing motion—love chosen daily against duty, weathered rather than solved.
